title: HE KILLED A MAN, RAN AWAY, AND THOUGHT HIS STORY WAS OVER. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME.
paragraphs: HE KILLED A MAN, RAN AWAY, AND THOUGHT HIS STORY WAS OVER. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME.

Before Moses stood before Pharaoh, before the sea opened, before a nation followed him into freedom, there was blood in the sand, a frightened fugitive in the wilderness, and forty years of silence. If you have ever wondered whether the worst thing you have done has permanently disqualified you from being used by God, do not leave this story too quickly.
There was a body in the sand.
And Moses knew exactly who put it there.

Before we turn him into stained glass, before we picture the staff raised over the Red Sea, before we remember the plagues, the Passover, Sinai, and the Ten Commandments, Scripture forces us to meet Moses somewhere far less comfortable.
At the scene of his failure.
A Hebrew man is being beaten by an Egyptian.
Exodus 2:12 records the terrifying sequence with almost cinematic simplicity:
He struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
There is something especially revealing about what happens immediately before the killing.
Scripture says Moses “looked this way and that way.”
The man who would one day stand publicly before Pharaoh was, at this moment, looking around to see who might be watching.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being merely Moses' story.
Because some of us know what it means to look this way and that way.
Before doing something we would desperately prefer nobody ever discover.
And somewhere inside us, we begin behaving as though the absence of human witnesses means the absence of God.
But there is always Someone we forget to look toward.
Moses buried the Egyptian beneath the sand.
And human beings have been burying things ever since.
We bury addictions beneath respectable appearances.
We bury resentment beneath church attendance.
We bury secret compromises beneath Bible verses posted publicly.
We bury spiritual exhaustion beneath “I’m blessed.”
We learn how to smile while standing over graves nobody else knows exist.
Perhaps there is something in your past that still makes your stomach tighten when you remember it.
Perhaps your failure is not ancient history.
Perhaps you have asked God for forgiveness and still cannot imagine how He could ever use someone who did what you did.
Because the sand did not finish Moses' story.
The next day Moses discovers that his secret is not secret.
Two Hebrews are fighting. Moses intervenes, and one of them fires a sentence directly into the place Moses hoped nobody could see:
“Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian?”
The blood beneath the sand suddenly has a voice.
Pharaoh hears about the killing and seeks to kill him.

Acts 7 later confirms the event plainly: Moses killed the Egyptian, and after his deed became known, he fled to Midian. Stephen's speech also gives us an important detail about Moses' thinking: Moses apparently believed his fellow Israelites would understand that God was giving them deliverance through him, but they did not.
Moses appears to have had some awareness that his life was connected to Israel's deliverance.
But calling and timing are not the same thing.
A God-given concern does not justify a flesh-driven method.
But God did not need Moses to become a murderer to accomplish it.
That distinction protects us from a dangerous distortion of this story.
The Bible is not saying, “Moses murdered somebody, so apparently sin does not matter.”
Grace does not require us to rename evil as good.
Grace is infinitely more beautiful than that.
Grace says God can confront what was evil without surrendering the person who committed it to hopelessness.
Moses runs from Egypt into Midian.
We read those words in seconds.
Moses lived them one sunrise at a time.
There are people reading this who understand that wilderness more than they wish they did.
You thought God was going to use you by now.
You thought the marriage would be healed by now.
You thought the prayer would have been answered by now.
You thought you would have overcome that struggle by now.
You thought your children would have returned to God by now.
You thought the door would have opened.
You thought the grief would hurt less.
You thought your life would look different.
Instead, you are feeding sheep in a chapter you never planned to enter.
And the frightening thought begins whispering:
Maybe this is all my life will ever be.
Maybe the thing I did disqualified me.
Maybe God uses people like Moses...
Then one ordinary day, a bush burns.
And from inside the fire comes something he may never have expected to hear again.
The Hebrew of Exodus 3:4 is breathtakingly personal:
God knew exactly who He was calling.
God did not discover Moses' history after calling him.
There was no embarrassing file heaven forgot to check.
And God called his name anyway.
That does not make Moses innocent.
There is a difference between God excusing a person's past and God redeeming a person's life.
Biblical grace never says sin is insignificant.

Biblical grace says sin is so serious that redemption ultimately requires blood—and the blood that finally answers humanity's guilt is not the blood Moses spilled in Egypt, but the blood Jesus Christ willingly shed at Calvary.
That is where Moses' story begins pointing beyond Moses.
The deliverer of Israel needed a greater Deliverer.

Hebrews makes the Christ-centered dimension of Moses' faith explicit. It says that Moses chose suffering with God's people over the temporary pleasures associated with Egypt and regarded the reproach connected with Christ—the Messiah—as greater treasure than Egypt's riches.
Moses led slaves out of Egypt.
Jesus liberates sinners from slavery to sin.
Moses stretched out his hand and Israel passed through the sea.
Jesus stretched out His hands on a cross and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
In Jesus Christ we behold the One who perfectly fulfills God's righteous purpose and bears the curse sinners could never remove from themselves.
And here is where this story becomes painfully personal.
You may be trying to bury what Jesus came to redeem.
You may have spent years running from a God who already knows where you are.
You may think repentance means approaching Christ with information He has not heard yet.
It is coming into the light and saying:
And the Gospel does not answer the repentant sinner with self-improvement.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin never happened.
He demonstrates exactly how serious sin is.
Christ, the sinless Son of God, gives Himself for sinners.
Forgiveness is purchased at terrible cost.
And because Jesus rose from the dead, failure does not have to write the final sentence over anyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Moses' story certainly does not teach that.
Grace is not a time machine.
You may not be able to undo what happened.
You may need to make restitution where appropriate.
You may need to accept consequences.
Some relationships may require years to rebuild.
Consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, condemnation does not own the final word.
And perhaps the most extraordinary thing about Moses is that God did not merely forgive a broken man and leave him hidden in Midian.
Back toward the geography of his fear.
Imagine Moses walking toward the place from which he once fled.
Years earlier, Moses had acted in his own strength and buried one Egyptian.
Now God would display His power and lead an enslaved nation toward freedom.
Moses once looked this way and that way before acting.
Later, Hebrews remembers him as a man who endured by looking toward the One who is invisible.
Faith taught him to live by a greater reality:
The man who ran from Pharaoh would return to confront Pharaoh.
The man who hid a body would stand openly before a king.
The man who believed his usefulness had collapsed would become an instrument through whom God displayed extraordinary deliverance.
But do not turn this into the shallow slogan, “Your mess automatically becomes your ministry.”
Not every failure leads to a platform.
Not every redeemed person becomes famous.
Not every wilderness ends with public prominence.
Sometimes grace leads you into a quiet life of faithful obedience that nobody applauds.
The treasure is not becoming another Moses.
The treasure is belonging to Christ.
The greatest miracle in this story is not that Moses eventually became important.
The greatest miracle is that the Holy God speaks to sinful human beings at all.
And this is why somebody reading this needs to stop saying:
“God could never want me after what I've done.”
Be careful about finishing a sentence God has not finished writing.
David's history contains adultery, deception, and bloodshed.
None of their sins became virtues.
Yet none proved stronger than God's redemptive purpose.
And your sin is not made harmless by grace either.
It must be brought to Christ.
Placed beneath the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
Maybe you have been in Midian emotionally for years.
But somewhere deep inside, you have quietly sentenced yourself.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You preach grace to everyone except the person in your mirror.
Then perhaps the question is no longer whether your past is ugly.
Perhaps it is whether you believe Christ's cross is sufficient.
The Gospel says that those who belong to Christ receive a new identity rooted not in their worst moment but in Him.
Your shame keeps pointing toward the sand.
And the cross is not permission to continue sinning.
It is the place where the sinner dies to the fantasy that sin can save, satisfy, or define him and begins learning to walk in newness of life.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Not when you feel worthy enough to pray.
Trust His finished work rather than your ability to compensate for your past.
And then walk where obedience leads.
Maybe somebody reading this is thinking:
“But you don't know what I did.”
The One inviting sinners to repentance is not working with incomplete information.
Christ knew the cost when He went to the cross.
Someone else may be sitting in their own Midian believing restoration is impossible, and God may use your testimony to remind them that grace is real.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, and every act of Christian service must flow from grace rather than attempt to purchase it.
Put it where the person who would never walk into your church might still read it at 1:17 in the morning.
Send it privately to the believer who disappeared because shame convinced him he could never come home.
Your good deeds cannot save you.
God knew the whole story before He spoke the name.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be torn from the book.
Maybe there is blood beneath your sand.
Maybe there are decades you call wasted.
Maybe you ran farther than you ever intended.
Maybe you no longer recognize the person staring back from the mirror.
Do not make peace with sin.
Do not hide what needs to be confessed.
But do not declare yourself beyond the reach of the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners and whose resurrection announces that death itself does not get the final word.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the shame to the cross.
Because Moses' greatest moment was not when everybody finally knew his name.
It was when, after all those years of running, he discovered that God still did.
You may have buried your past in the sand, but Jesus was already preparing a road through the sea.
